mechanism_of_action.source_excerpt: Section 12.1 Mechanism of Action -- full text: "The mechanism of action of immunoglobulins in the treatment of chronic ITP or in Dermatomyositis has not been fully elucidated." Octagam 10% is a solvent/detergent-treated, chromatographically purified human immunoglobulin G (IgG) preparation manufactured from large pools of human plasma (Description, Section 11) -- a plasma-derived polyclonal antibody product, not a monoclonal antibody, fusion protein, or small molecule.

value.title: THROMBOSIS, RENAL DYSFUNCTION, AND ACUTE RENAL FAILURE

boxed_warning.source_excerpt: Boxed warning full text: "Thrombosis may occur with immune globulin intravenous (IGIV) products, including Octagam 10%. Risk factors may include: advanced age, prolonged immobilization, hypercoagulable conditions, history of venous or arterial thrombosis, use of estrogens, indwelling vascular catheters, hyperviscosity, and cardiovascular risk factors. Thrombosis may occur in the absence of known risk factors. (See WARNING AND PRECAUTIONS [5.5], PATIENT COUNSELING INFORMATION [17]) / Renal dysfunction, acute renal failure, osmotic nephropathy, and death may occur in predisposed patients who receive IGIV products, including Octagam 10%... For patients at risk of thrombosis, renal dysfunction or acute renal failure, administer Octagam 10% at the minimum dose and infusion rate practicable." Patients with dermatomyositis specifically are called out (Section 5.5) as being "at increased risk for thromboembolic events" requiring an infusion rate cap of 0.04 mL/kg/min, lower than the ITP indication's cap. Renal dysfunction/acute renal failure has no matching entry in this schema's WARNING_CATEGORIES enum (serious_infections/mortality/malignancy/mace/thrombosis/suicidal_ideation/hepatotoxicity/embryo_fetal_toxicity) -- recorded in the title and referenced_label_sections but not double-counted as a category.

faers_summary.source_excerpt: openFDA drug/event.json aggregate for "OCTAGAM": total_reports=1969, serious=1554, deaths=124, hospitalizations=678. Ran the atlas's standard drugindication count check before accepting the term (per AGENTS.md's Qbrexza/Glycopyrronium and Xepi/Ozenoxacin precedent): OCTAGAM's FAERS reports are dominated by its original, much broader ITP/general-immunodeficiency off-label uses -- top drugindication terms are "PRODUCT USED FOR UNKNOWN INDICATION" (344+319), HYPOGAMMAGLOBULINAEMIA (116/39), IMMUNODEFICIENCY COMMON VARIABLE (99/43), CHRONIC INFLAMMATORY DEMYELINATING POLYRADICULONEUROPATHY (82/41), HEREDITARY ANGIOEDEMA (77), PLASMA CELL MYELOMA (56/45), MYASTHENIA GRAVIS (48) -- dermatomyositis does not appear in the top 15 terms at all. Unlike Qbrexza/Ozenoxacin, there is no separate brand-vs-generic split to retry (Octagam is a single product traded under one name, not generic+brand) and no alternate clean search term exists -- this is a real, unavoidable mix across every indication the product is used for, the same "no clean term available" situation as Ruxolitinib, recorded as-is rather than picking a term that looks cleaner.

drug_characterization.source_excerpt: Computed by pulling every individual FAERS report matching this drug's own search_term (OCTAGAM) and tallying each report's drugcharacterization code (1=suspect, 2=concomitant, 3=interacting) from ONLY the drug-array entries whose medicinalproduct matches this drug (not co-listed drugs in the same report) -- a plain count= aggregate query cannot do this correctly (openFDA's flattened array indexing mixes in co-listed drugs' own characterization values). 1969/1969 reports matched.
